sources.title: UCL module catalogue 2026/27: POLS0006 Introduction to Politics

about: A 30-credit foundation course in the concepts used to study politics, taught across Terms 1 and 2 and core for BSc Philosophy, Politics and Economics. It distinguishes explanatory theories of how politics works from normative theories of how it ought to work, and stresses connecting theory to evidence. The 2026/27 catalogue lists indicative topics (the state, power, democracy, collective action) and assessment of 25% coursework and 75% exam. This pack adds a framing topic on theory and evidence and treats democracy in two parts.
topics: Explanatory and normative theory: linking theory to evidence

notes.h: Explanatory and normative theory: linking theory to evidence
notes.body:
Politics can be studied in two broad ways. Explanatory (positive, empirical) theories ask how the political world is and why: why do some countries become democracies, why do citizens vote, why do states tax? Normative theories ask how the political world ought to be: what makes a government legitimate, what is a just distribution of resources, is democracy better than rule by experts? Introduction to Politics is built on this distinction and on the skill of connecting the two to evidence.

The is/ought gap
David Hume (A Treatise of Human Nature, 1739-40) noted that writers often slide from statements about what is to statements about what ought to be without explaining the step. Facts alone do not entail values: that most people obey the law does not show they ought to. Yet the two are linked. Normative arguments rest on empirical assumptions (an argument for compulsory voting assumes it raises turnout without harming the quality of decisions), and empirical research is usually motivated by normative concerns.

Building an explanation
- A concept is an abstract category such as "democracy" or "power". It must be defined clearly and measured validly: does the indicator capture what the concept means?
- A hypothesis links an independent variable (the proposed cause) to a dependent variable (the outcome). A mechanism explains how the cause produces the effect.
- Correlation is not causation. An association may be produced by a confounder (a third variable that causes both), by reverse causation, or by selection effects.
- Causal claims are counterfactual: the effect of a cause is the difference between what happened and what would have happened without it. We can never observe both for the same unit at the same time, which Paul Holland (1986) called the fundamental problem of causal inference.

Strategies for causal inference
- Randomised experiments assign the cause at random, so treated and control groups are comparable on average.
- Natural experiments use events that assign cases as if at random (Dunning, 2012).
- Comparative case studies use John Stuart Mill's methods of agreement and difference (A System of Logic, 1843). Statistical controls try to hold confounders constant but cannot control what is unmeasured.
- Karl Popper (Logik der Forschung, 1934; English translation 1959) argued that a scientific theory must be falsifiable. Social science rarely delivers decisive refutations, so evidence is usually weighed cumulatively.

Evaluating normative arguments
Normative arguments are assessed through the clarity of their premises, internal consistency and fit with considered judgements. Thought experiments are common tools: Rawls's original position (A Theory of Justice, 1971) asks what principles we would choose behind a veil of ignorance, and he describes testing principles against intuitions as seeking reflective equilibrium. Feasibility also matters: a theory that demands what people cannot do invites the objection that ought implies can.

Putting them together
Many of the best questions combine both. "Democracy is justified because it produces good outcomes" is a normative claim with an empirical premise; you can assess the premise with evidence (for example, comparative work on famines or public goods) and the claim by asking whether outcomes are the right standard (an alternative is that democracy is valuable because it treats people as equals).

Exam tips: name the type of claim you are discussing before you assess it; never treat a correlation as a cause without discussing confounders; and when you cite a theory, say what evidence would count for or against it.

The state is the central unit of modern politics, yet defining it is contested. The most influential definition is Max Weber's, from his 1919 lecture "Politics as a Vocation": a state is a human community that successfully claims the monopoly of the legitimate use of physical force within a given territory. Three features matter: territory, a claim to a monopoly of force and the claim to legitimacy. Weber distinguished three ideal types of legitimate authority (Economy and Society, 1922): traditional (custom), charismatic (devotion to an exceptional leader) and legal-rational (impersonal rules and offices), the last typical of modern bureaucratic states.

Juridical statehood is often tested against the Montevideo Convention (1933), which lists a permanent population, a defined territory, a government and capacity to enter relations with other states. Do not confuse the state with the nation (a community that sees itself as sharing identity) or with the government (the group currently holding office).

Why do states exist? Contract theories
Thomas Hobbes (Leviathan, 1651) imagines a state of nature without common power, a war of all against all, and argues that rational individuals would submit to a sovereign to escape it. John Locke (Two Treatises of Government, 1689) argues that people in the state of nature have natural rights and the state exists to protect life, liberty and property, so it is limited and can be resisted if it breaks trust. Robert Nozick (Anarchy, State, and Utopia, 1974) defends a minimal state limited to protection against force, theft and fraud.

Other explanatory accounts
- Marxist view: the state is the instrument of the dominant class; the Communist Manifesto (1848) describes the modern state as a committee for managing the common affairs of the bourgeoisie.
- Pluralist view: the state is an arena in which competing groups bargain (Dahl, Who Governs?, 1961).
- Charles Tilly: "war made the state, and the state made war" (1975, in his chapter in The Formation of National States in Western Europe), an argument he developed in Coercion, Capital, and European States (1990). Rulers preparing for war needed taxes and administrators, which built state capacity in early modern Europe.
- Mancur Olson (1993) contrasted the roving bandit, who plunders, with the stationary bandit, who has an interest in a productive economy and so provides order.

State capacity and strength
Michael Mann (1984) distinguished despotic power (the elite's ability to act without negotiation with society) from infrastructural power (the ability to penetrate society and implement decisions). A state can be despotically weak yet infrastructurally strong, as many liberal democracies are. Francis Fukuyama emphasises capacity, rule of law and accountability. Weak or failing states cannot secure a monopoly of force, creating space for warlords or militias. Acemoglu and Robinson (Why Nations Fail, 2012) argue that inclusive institutions drive prosperity, though their historical claims are debated.

The state and sovereignty
The 1648 Peace of Westphalia is often credited with creating the sovereign state system, but many historians regard this as a myth, since sovereignty developed gradually. Modern states also face challenges from supranational bodies (the EU), globalised markets and sub-state nationalism.

Exam tips: define the state before using it, say which theory you favour and why, and use evidence (Tilly for Europe) while noting that the European path does not fit every region.

Power is the central concept of political science and one of its most contested. Debate usually proceeds through "faces" or dimensions of power.

First dimension: decision-making power
Robert Dahl (1957, "The Concept of Power") defined power in intuitive terms: A has power over B to the extent that A can get B to do something that B would not otherwise do. In Who Governs? (1961) he studied key decisions in New Haven (urban redevelopment, public education and party nominations) and found that different groups prevailed in different areas, supporting pluralism: power is dispersed, not held by a single elite. The method is behavioural: observe who participates in decisions and who wins when preferences conflict. It contrasts with Floyd Hunter's reputational approach (Community Power Structure, 1953) and C. Wright Mills's The Power Elite (1956), which saw power concentrated.

Second dimension: agenda-setting
Peter Bachrach and Morton Baratz (1962, "Two Faces of Power") argued that Dahl missed the power to keep issues off the agenda. Power is also exercised when A devotes energy to creating or reinforcing barriers so that conflicts remain unspoken, what they called non-decision-making. E. E. Schattschneider (The Semisovereign People, 1960) captured the same idea: every organisation has a mobilisation of bias that favours some conflicts and suppresses others. A study of decisions alone will therefore underestimate the power of those whose interests are protected by the agenda.

Third dimension: shaping preferences
Steven Lukes (Power: A Radical View, 1974; 2nd edition 2005) added a third dimension: A may exercise power over B by influencing, shaping or determining B's wants, so that B does not even perceive grievances. Lukes argued that there may be a latent conflict between the wants of those with power and the real interests of those they exclude. John Gaventa (Power and Powerlessness, 1980) illustrated this with quiescence in an Appalachian mining community. The critique is that identifying "real interests" risks arrogance: who decides what people really want, and how can it be tested?

Other approaches
- Michel Foucault (Discipline and Punish, 1975; English 1977) treats power as diffuse and productive: it works through institutions, norms and knowledge (power/knowledge) that create subjects, not only repress them.
- Hannah Arendt (On Violence, 1970) separates power, which arises when people act in concert, from violence, which is instrumental.
- Joseph Nye (1990) distinguished hard power (coercion and payment) from soft power (attraction through culture, values and policies).
- Structural power concerns the ability to shape the framework in which others operate (as in Susan Strange's work on finance, production, security and knowledge structures).

Power over and power to
Many theorists distinguish power over (A controls B) from power to (capacity to achieve goals, possibly collectively). Thinking only of domination misses the way collective action can generate power.

Exam tips: for each dimension, give an author, a definition and an example; evaluate by asking what evidence each view needs and whether it can be tested; avoid treating the dimensions as one replacing the next, since Lukes builds on the earlier two.

Democracy literally means rule by the people (demos, people; kratos, rule), but the idea is contested. Introduction to Politics asks both what democracy is and why, if at all, it is valuable. Different theories answer differently.

Direct, representative and minimal democracy
- Direct democracy: citizens decide laws themselves, as in ancient Athens' assembly (Athens excluded women, slaves and foreigners from citizenship). Jean-Jacques Rousseau (The Social Contract, 1762) argued that sovereignty is the exercise of the general will and cannot be represented.
- Representative democracy: citizens choose representatives. James Madison (Federalist No. 10, 1787) contrasted a republic with a pure democracy, arguing that representation could refine the public's views and control faction in a large state. John Stuart Mill (Considerations on Representative Government, 1861) defended representative government and proportional representation, and valued participation for its educative effect.
- Minimal (competitive elite) democracy: Joseph Schumpeter (Capitalism, Socialism and Democracy, 1942) rejected the "classical doctrine" that there is a common good the people decide. For him democracy is a method: an institutional arrangement in which individuals acquire power through a competitive struggle for the people's vote. Its virtues are peaceful turnover and accountability.

Polyarchy
Robert Dahl (Polyarchy, 1971) proposed that real democracies, which he called polyarchies, are defined by two dimensions: public contestation (the right to oppose the government, with free and fair elections, free expression and alternative information) and inclusiveness (the share of adults entitled to take part). In later work (Democracy and Its Critics, 1989) Dahl listed seven institutions of polyarchy: elected officials, free and fair elections, inclusive suffrage, the right to run for office, freedom of expression, alternative sources of information and associational autonomy.

Participatory and deliberative theories
- Carole Pateman (Participation and Democratic Theory, 1970) criticised minimal democracy for neglecting participation, arguing that taking part in decisions, including in the workplace, develops citizens' abilities.
- Deliberative democrats such as Jurgen Habermas, Joshua Cohen (1989) and Amy Gutmann and Dennis Thompson (1996) say democratic legitimacy comes from public reasoning among free and equal citizens, not only from aggregating votes.

Epistemic arguments and challenges
- The Marquis de Condorcet (1785) showed that if each voter is more than 50 per cent likely to be right and votes independently, the majority becomes more likely to be right as the group grows. Critics note the assumptions are demanding.
- Jason Brennan (Against Democracy, 2016) argues for epistocracy, rule by the knowledgeable, because many voters are uninformed; opponents say this lacks fair procedure and risks bias in who counts as expert.
- Arrow's impossibility theorem (1951) shows no ranked voting system satisfies a small set of reasonable conditions, and William Riker (1982) used social choice results to question the idea of a coherent "will of the people".
- Tocqueville (Democracy in America, 1835 and 1840) warned of the tyranny of the majority, hence the idea that democracy needs rights as well as votes.

Why value democracy?
Instrumental arguments claim it produces good outcomes, for instance Amartya Sen's argument that famines do not occur in functioning democracies (Development as Freedom, 1999). Intrinsic arguments claim that treating people as equals requires giving them an equal say.

Exam tips: distinguish what democracy is (definitions) from why it is valuable (justifications); use Schumpeter and Dahl as your anchors; and be ready to say what each theory implies for institutions.

This topic turns from what democracy should be to explaining where it exists and how institutions shape it. Evidence is contested at almost every step.

Modernisation theory
Seymour Martin Lipset (1959, "Some Social Requisites of Democracy") argued that economic development makes democracy more likely: wealth, education and urbanisation moderate conflict and create a middle class. The correlation between income and democracy is strong. But Adam Przeworski and Fernando Limongi (1997, "Modernization: Theories and Facts") distinguished two readings. On the endogenous reading, development causes transitions to democracy; on the exogenous reading, transitions happen for other reasons, but once democracy exists it is much more likely to survive in rich countries. Their data (Przeworski et al., Democracy and Development, 2000) supported the exogenous view: democracies in countries with high income per head almost never fell, while income had little power to predict transitions. Others dispute this. Carles Boix (2003) and Daron Acemoglu and James Robinson (2006) model democratisation as bargaining over redistribution and elite fear of revolution. Barrington Moore (Social Origins of Dictatorship and Democracy, 1966) stressed class coalitions and the path through which agrarian societies industrialised. Samuel Huntington (The Third Wave, 1991) described waves of democratisation, the latest beginning in Portugal in 1974.

Presidential and parliamentary systems
Juan Linz (1990, "The Perils of Presidentialism") argued that presidential systems have dual democratic legitimacy and fixed terms, which make deadlock and breakdown more likely than in parliamentary systems, where the government depends on the legislature's confidence. José Antonio Cheibub (2007) disputed this, arguing that breakdowns owe more to the military and to the kind of country in which presidentialism is chosen.

Electoral systems
- Plurality (first past the post) in single-member districts: the candidate with most votes wins.
- Proportional representation (PR): seats are allocated roughly in proportion to votes.
- Duverger (1951): plurality tends to produce two-party competition because voters avoid wasting votes and parties merge; PR tends to support multiple parties. Gary Cox (1997) generalised this: in districts electing M members, only about M + 1 candidates are viable.
- Plurality can produce disproportionate outcomes and sometimes a hung parliament, as in the UK in 2010.

Majoritarian and consensus democracy
Arend Lijphart (Patterns of Democracy, 1999) classified 36 democracies by the extent to which power is concentrated (majoritarian, "Westminster") or shared (consensus), along two dimensions: executives-parties (party system, electoral system, coalition) and federal-unitary. He found that consensus democracies perform at least as well on economic management and better on representation of women and satisfaction with democracy, although critics question the data and methods.

Veto players
George Tsebelis (2002) argued that policy change is harder the more actors (such as chambers, coalition partners and courts) must agree and the further apart their positions.

Democratic backsliding
Recent literature emphasises erosion by elected leaders rather than coups (Bermeo, 2016; Levitsky and Ziblatt, 2018). Annual indices from V-Dem and Freedom House are used to track this; their figures change each year, so check the latest report.

Exam tips: present modernisation as contested, separate the question of why democracies arise from why they last, and tie institutions to mechanisms.

A collective action problem arises when individuals who would all benefit from cooperation have incentives not to contribute. It underlies the provision of public goods, the management of shared resources and the organisation of groups. It is central to explaining why states exist, why movements succeed or fail and why environmental protection is hard.

Public goods and free-riding
A public good is non-excludable (people cannot be prevented from benefiting) and non-rival (one person's use does not reduce another's). Examples are national defence, clean air and public order. Because people can enjoy the good whether or not they pay, each has an incentive to free-ride, and the good may be under-provided.

The prisoner's dilemma
In the prisoner's dilemma (formalised by Flood and Dresher in 1950 and named by Albert Tucker), each of two players is better off defecting whatever the other does, but both are worse off when both defect than when both cooperate. Defection is a dominant strategy, so the equilibrium of a one-shot game is mutual defection. Other structures matter: in an assurance (stag hunt) game, cooperation is an equilibrium if you expect others to cooperate. Robert Axelrod (The Evolution of Cooperation, 1984) showed that in repeated games, strategies such as tit-for-tat can sustain cooperation when players expect to meet again and value the future.

Olson's logic
Mancur Olson (The Logic of Collective Action, 1965) overturned the assumption that groups with shared interests will naturally act on them. In large groups, each member's contribution makes a negligible difference and monitoring is hard, so rational individuals free-ride. Small groups are "privileged": each member has a large stake. Large groups can organise only if they offer selective incentives (benefits available only to contributors, such as insurance from a union) or use coercion (such as compulsory membership). Critics note that Olson struggles to explain why people join protests and movements anyway, which may reflect moral commitment, identity or social networks.

The tragedy of the commons
Garrett Hardin (1968, Science) argued that a shared resource like pasture is overused because each herder gains fully from adding an animal while the cost is shared. His solutions were privatisation or state control. Elinor Ostrom (Governing the Commons, 1990; Nobel Prize in Economics 2009, shared with Oliver Williamson) showed with case studies that communities often manage common-pool resources through their own institutions. Her design principles include clear boundaries, rules suited to local conditions, monitoring, graduated sanctions and conflict-resolution mechanisms.

The paradox of voting
Anthony Downs (1957) noted that a single vote is very unlikely to be decisive. In Riker and Ordeshook's calculus of voting (1968), a person votes if pB - C + D > 0, where p is the probability of being decisive, B the benefit of the preferred outcome winning, C the cost of voting and D a duty or expressive benefit. Since p is tiny, D does much of the explanatory work.

Solutions to collective action problems
- The state: Hobbes saw the sovereign as enforcing cooperation; taxes fund public goods.
- Selective incentives, social norms and reputation.
- Repeated interaction and monitoring, as in Ostrom's cases.
- Social capital and trust (Putnam, 1993).
- Threshold models (Granovetter, 1978): people join when enough others have, explaining sudden mobilisation.

Exam tips: label the game structure, not only the example; give Olson and Ostrom as contrasting views; and note that rational choice explanations can be supplemented, not only rejected.

cards.b: Normative theory asks how politics ought to be (legitimacy, justice); explanatory (positive) theory asks how it is and why. Good arguments often combine both, as normative claims rest on empirical premises.
Hume (Treatise, 1739-40): you cannot validly derive a statement of what ought to be solely from statements of what is; a value premise is needed.
A third variable that causes both the supposed cause and the outcome, producing a misleading correlation (e.g. hot weather raising both ice-cream sales and drownings).
Holland (1986): we cannot observe the same unit both treated and untreated, so the counterfactual is unobserved and must be estimated by comparison.
A real-world event assigns cases to conditions as if at random, so comparing them approximates an experiment without the researcher randomising (Dunning, 2012).
Mill (1843): the method of agreement looks for the one factor shared by cases with the same outcome; the method of difference compares otherwise similar cases that differ in outcome.
Popper (1934; 1959 in English): a theory is scientific only if some possible observation could refute it. Critics say social theories are rarely tested decisively.
Rawls (1971): adjusting principles and particular considered judgements until they cohere. It is a method for testing normative theories.
A human community that successfully claims the monopoly of the legitimate use of physical force within a given territory (Politics as a Vocation, 1919).
Traditional (custom), charismatic (devotion to an exceptional leader), legal-rational (impersonal rules and offices); the modern bureaucratic state rests on legal-rational authority.
A permanent population, a defined territory, a government, and capacity to enter relations with other states.
'War made the state, and the state made war' (Tilly 1975; developed in Coercion, Capital, and European States, 1990): preparing for war pushed European rulers to tax and build bureaucracies.
Mann (1984): despotic power is the elite's freedom to act without bargaining with society; infrastructural power is the capacity to penetrate society and implement decisions.

cards.f: Hobbes vs Locke on the state
cards.b: Hobbes (1651): the state of nature is a war of all, justifying a strong sovereign. Locke (1689): natural rights are protected by a limited state that can be resisted if it betrays trust.
Nozick (1974): the only justified state is limited to protecting against force, theft and fraud and enforcing contracts; wider redistribution violates individual rights.
State: territorial political organisation with a monopoly of legitimate force. Nation: a community with a sense of shared identity. Government: those currently running the state.
A has power over B to the extent that A can get B to do something B would not otherwise do; studied through observable decision-making and winners and losers.
Who Governs? studied New Haven and found that different groups prevailed on different issues, so power was dispersed rather than concentrated in one elite.
Bachrach and Baratz (1962): power to keep issues off the agenda (non-decision-making), so that potential conflicts never become decisions.
Schattschneider (1960): institutions and practices favour some interests and conflicts and suppress others, shaping what gets onto the agenda.
Lukes (1974): A shapes B's wants and beliefs so B does not see its grievances; the conflict is latent, between wants and 'real interests'.
Identifying people's 'real interests' appears paternalistic and hard to test; who judges what citizens would want if free of influence?
Power is diffuse and productive, working through institutions, norms and knowledge (power/knowledge) to shape subjects rather than only repress them.
Nye (1990): the ability to get preferred outcomes through attraction (culture, values, policies) instead of coercion or payment (hard power).
Capitalism, Socialism and Democracy (1942): an institutional method in which individuals gain power by competing for the people's votes; rejects the idea of a pre-existing common good.
Real-world democracy defined by two dimensions: public contestation (opposition, free and fair elections) and inclusiveness (share of adults who can participate).
The general will cannot be represented; sovereignty is exercised by citizens themselves (Social Contract, 1762).
Federalist No. 10 (1787): representation in a large republic can refine public opinion and control faction better than direct democracy in a small society.
Pateman (1970): participation, including in the workplace, educates citizens; minimal democracy neglects this developmental value.
Legitimacy comes from public reasoning among free and equal citizens (Habermas, Cohen, Gutmann and Thompson), not merely from aggregating preferences by voting.
If each voter is independently more than 50% likely to be right, the chance that the majority is right rises with group size; assumptions are demanding.
Rule by the knowledgeable (Brennan, 2016). Objection: it may lack procedural fairness and who counts as an expert is itself disputed.
Economic development (wealth, education, urbanisation) makes democracy more likely by moderating conflict and building a middle class.
Income does not predict transitions to democracy well, but democracies in wealthier countries are far more likely to survive (exogenous reading; Przeworski et al., 2000).
Huntington (1991): the third wave of democratisation began in Portugal in 1974 and spread through Southern Europe, Latin America and elsewhere.
Plurality voting in single-member districts tends to produce two-party competition; PR tends to allow multiple parties (Duverger, 1951). It is a tendency, not a certainty.
Linz (1990): fixed terms and dual legitimacy in presidential systems make deadlock and breakdown more likely than in parliamentary systems; contested by Cheibub (2007).
Patterns of Democracy (1999): executives-parties and federal-unitary dimensions distinguish majoritarian from consensus democracies across 36 countries.
An individual or collective actor whose agreement is needed to change policy; Tsebelis (2002): more veto players with different positions mean more policy stability.
Gradual erosion of democratic institutions, often by elected leaders rather than coups; measured by indices such as V-Dem and Freedom House, which update annually.
Non-excludable and non-rival: people cannot be stopped from benefiting and one person's use does not reduce another's (national defence, clean air).
Individuals can enjoy a collective benefit without contributing, so each has an incentive not to pay, which can lead to under-provision.
Each player does better by defecting whatever the other does, yet mutual defection leaves both worse off than mutual cooperation. One-shot equilibrium: both defect.
Axelrod (1984): cooperate first, then copy the other's last move. It can sustain cooperation in repeated prisoner's dilemmas when the future matters.
Benefits or penalties available only to individuals who contribute, which can overcome free-riding in large groups (The Logic of Collective Action, 1965).
Hardin (1968): a shared resource is overused because users receive the full benefit of exploiting it but share the cost. Ostrom showed communities can avoid it.
Governing the Commons (1990): communities can manage common-pool resources through self-made rules, monitoring and graduated sanctions, without privatisation or state control.
Riker and Ordeshook (1968): vote if pB - C + D > 0. Since the chance p of being decisive is tiny, the duty or expressive term D explains much turnout.

questions.q: Which of these is a normative claim rather than an explanatory one?
options: Plurality voting in single-member districts tends to produce fewer parties than proportional representation.
Voters with more years of education are, on average, more likely to turn out.
Governments ought to prioritise reducing inequality over maximising growth.
Richer democracies are less likely to collapse than poorer ones.
questions.why: The claim about what governments ought to prioritise states a value judgement, which data alone cannot settle. The claims about plurality voting, education and turnout, and richer democracies are all empirical statements about how things are: evidence could confirm or refute them, so they are explanatory, even if some are contested.

questions.q: Countries with more ice-cream sales also have more drownings. What is the most plausible reading?
options: Drownings cause people to buy more ice cream.
The correlation proves the variables are causally unrelated.
A confounder, hot weather, raises both.
Eating ice cream causes drownings, perhaps through cramps.
questions.why: Warm weather means more swimming and more ice-cream eating, so a common cause produces the association. The idea that ice cream causes drowning treats correlation as causation; reverse causation (drownings raising sales) has no plausible mechanism; and the claim that the correlation proves the two are causally unrelated overreaches: a correlation on its own can neither prove nor rule out a causal link, so a third factor has to be argued for, not read off the data.

questions.q: Explain the 'fundamental problem of causal inference' and outline two ways political scientists try to address it.
markScheme: Defines the problem: a unit cannot be observed both with and without the cause at the same time (Holland, 1986)
Links to counterfactual definition of a causal effect
Randomised experiments: random assignment makes groups comparable on average
Natural experiments or matched comparisons (Mill's methods) approximating this
Notes limits, e.g. unobserved confounders, external validity, ethics
questions.modelAnswer: A causal effect is the difference between what happened to a unit and what would have happened had the cause been absent. Holland (1986) called our inability to observe both outcomes for the same unit at the same time the fundamental problem of causal inference: the counterfactual is always missing, so it must be estimated from other units. One solution is the randomised experiment. By assigning the cause at random, for example giving some voters a mobilisation message, the treated and control groups should be alike on average in all other respects, so differences in outcomes can be attributed to the treatment. A second is the natural experiment, where an event such as a lottery or an arbitrary boundary assigns units as if at random (Dunning, 2012); comparative case studies using Mill's method of difference also try to find cases that are similar except for the cause. Both have limits: experiments may be unethical or unrealistic, natural experiments depend on the as-if-random assumption, and matched comparisons cannot rule out unobserved confounders. Findings therefore need replication and a plausible mechanism.

questions.q: According to Weber, what defines the modern state?
options: Its role as the instrument through which the dominant economic class rules
A common language and culture shared by the population
A successful claim to the monopoly of the legitimate use of physical force within a territory
Possession of a written constitution and an elected government
questions.why: Weber's 1919 definition centres on the monopoly of legitimate force within a territory. A written constitution and elections describe a constitutional democracy, not every state. Common language and culture describe a nation, which is a different thing from a state. The instrument-of-the-dominant-class idea is the Marxist theory of what the state does, not Weber's definition.

questions.q: What is Charles Tilly's argument about state formation in Europe?
options: Fully formed bureaucratic states were needed before any state could fight wars
States arose to organise large-scale irrigation in river valleys
States emerged from a voluntary agreement among free and equal individuals
Rulers' need to finance war led them to build tax and administrative capacity
questions.why: Tilly argues that preparing for war drove extraction and administrative growth. The voluntary agreement story is a social contract thought experiment, not an historical explanation. Irrigation as the origin of centralised states is a different thesis (the hydraulic theory associated with Wittfogel). The claim that fully formed bureaucratic states were needed before any state could fight wars reverses Tilly's causal order: for him war helped create the bureaucracies rather than requiring them first.

questions.q: Distinguish Weber's definition of the state from the Marxist and pluralist views of what the state does.
markScheme: Weber: monopoly of legitimate force in a territory; defines by means, not ends
Weber's legitimacy types may be mentioned
Marxist: state serves the dominant class (Communist Manifesto, 1848)
Pluralist: state is an arena for competing groups (Dahl 1961)
Distinguishes definition from explanation of whose interests the state serves
questions.modelAnswer: Weber (1919) defines the state by its distinctive means rather than its ends: it successfully claims a monopoly of the legitimate use of physical force within a territory, and he identifies legal-rational authority as the basis of legitimacy in modern states. This is a definition, so it is silent about whose interests the state serves. Marxists answer that question by arguing that the state acts for the dominant class; the Communist Manifesto (1848) calls the executive of the modern state a committee for managing the common affairs of the bourgeoisie. Pluralists such as Dahl (Who Governs?, 1961) argue instead that power is dispersed among many groups, and the state is an arena in which they compete and bargain, with no single group permanently dominant. The three are therefore not rivals at the same level: Weber's definition can be combined with either a Marxist or a pluralist account of who controls the state.

questions.q: Which description matches the 'second face' of power?
options: Winning observable conflicts over decisions
Shaping what people want so that they do not see any grievance
Preventing issues from reaching the decision-making agenda
Attracting others through culture and values
questions.why: Bachrach and Baratz's second face is non-decision-making: keeping issues off the agenda. Winning visible conflicts is Dahl's first dimension. Shaping wants so that grievances are not perceived is Lukes's third dimension. Attraction through culture and values is Nye's soft power, a different concept altogether.

questions.q: Why did critics say Dahl's New Haven study could miss important power?
options: It looked only at decisions on issues that reached the agenda
It relied on reputations for influence rather than observed decisions
It found that a single elite controlled all decisions
The city was too small for any power relations to be visible
questions.why: Critics such as Bachrach and Baratz argued that studying only observable decisions ignores power exercised by keeping issues off the agenda. The reputational method is the elitist approach used by Hunter, which Dahl rejected in favour of observing decisions. Dahl's finding was pluralist, not that a single elite dominated. City size was not the objection raised.

questions.q: Outline Lukes's three-dimensional view of power, with an example of each dimension.
markScheme: First dimension: decision-making, observable conflict (Dahl) e.g. a council vote
Second dimension: agenda-setting, non-decisions (Bachrach and Baratz) e.g. issue never debated
Third dimension: preference shaping / ideological power (Lukes) e.g. workers accept low pay as natural
Notes Lukes sees them as cumulative, adding to the earlier views
Brief evaluation, e.g. 'real interests' problem
questions.modelAnswer: Lukes (1974) argues that power has three dimensions. The first, associated with Dahl, concerns observable decision-making in conflicts of interest: for example, which side wins a council vote on a new road. The second, from Bachrach and Baratz (1962), concerns control of the agenda: power is exercised when an issue, such as pollution from a local factory, is kept from being debated because the powerful can block it or because rules and procedures favour some interests. The third dimension concerns the shaping of preferences: power is exercised when A influences what B wants or believes, so that B accepts a situation as natural and does not articulate any grievance, for example workers who never question low pay because it is seen as inevitable. Lukes presents these as cumulative: each adds a layer to the earlier view rather than replacing it. A major criticism of the third dimension is that it relies on identifying people's real interests, which seems hard to establish without being paternalistic.

questions.q: Which theorist defined democracy as a competitive method for choosing leaders and rejected a pre-given 'common good'?
options: Joseph Schumpeter
Jean-Jacques Rousseau
Carole Pateman
John Stuart Mill
questions.why: Schumpeter (1942) is the minimal, competitive-elite theorist. Rousseau holds the opposite view, that there is a general will for the common good. Pateman is a participatory theorist who criticised minimal democracy. Mill valued participation and representative government for the development of citizens, so is also not a minimalist.

questions.q: In Dahl's account of polyarchy, which pair of dimensions are used?
options: Participation and deliberation
Liberty and equality of outcome
Majority rule and protection of minority rights
Public contestation and inclusiveness
questions.why: Dahl's two dimensions in Polyarchy (1971) are public contestation and inclusiveness. Majority rule versus minority rights is a different tension, discussed by Madison and Tocqueville. Participation and deliberation relate to the participatory and deliberative theories that came later. Liberty and equality of outcome are broad values; they are not Dahl's defining dimensions.

questions.q: Compare Schumpeter's minimal conception of democracy with a participatory critique of it.
markScheme: Schumpeter: democracy as competitive method for choosing leaders, 1942
Rejection of the 'common good' and of the competent citizen
Participatory critique (Pateman 1970): minimal view ignores developmental value of participation
Participation (incl. workplace) educates and builds capacities
Evaluation: realism and stability v. thin account of citizenship
questions.modelAnswer: Schumpeter (1942) argued that the classical doctrine of democracy, with a common good that citizens decide, is unrealistic because voters are poorly informed and open to manipulation. Democracy should be understood as a method: individuals compete for power by seeking the people's votes. Its value lies in peaceful change of leaders and accountability, not in citizen self-rule. Participatory theorists such as Pateman (1970) argue that this makes democracy too thin. Drawing on Rousseau and Mill, she holds that participation develops people's political capacities and sense of responsibility, so democracy should extend beyond voting to institutions such as the workplace. The minimalist can reply that high participation demands are unrealistic and that competitive elections provide a stable safeguard against tyranny; the participatory theorist responds that low participation may reflect the limited opportunities which minimal democracy itself provides. The disagreement is therefore partly about what democracy is for: protecting citizens, or developing them.

questions.q: What did Przeworski and Limongi (1997) conclude about income and democracy?
options: Democracies are more likely to collapse in wealthy countries
Rising incomes reliably cause dictatorships to become democracies
Democracy reliably causes faster economic growth
Higher income makes democracy more likely to survive, but does not reliably trigger transitions to it
questions.why: Their exogenous reading holds that transitions happen for other reasons but that wealthy democracies are very resilient. The claim that rising incomes reliably cause transitions is the endogenous version of modernisation theory that they reject. Democracy causing growth is a separate question on which they find no clear effect. The claim that democracies are more likely to collapse in wealthy countries reverses their result, since survival is more likely in richer countries.

questions.q: According to Duverger's law, which system tends to produce two-party competition?
options: Plurality voting in single-member districts
Proportional representation with large districts
Presidentialism, regardless of the electoral system
Any system with compulsory voting
questions.why: Plurality in single-member districts penalises small parties, so voters and elites coordinate on two. Proportional representation tends to allow more parties, so that is the opposite of the law. Presidentialism concerns the executive format, not the electoral rule. Compulsory voting changes turnout but does not create the coordination pressure behind Duverger's argument.

questions.q: Explain the debate between Lipset's modernisation theory and Przeworski and Limongi's critique.
markScheme: Lipset (1959): development increases the likelihood of democracy
Endogenous reading: development produces transitions
Przeworski and Limongi (1997): exogenous reading; transitions are not explained by income
But income strongly helps democracy survive
Notes alternative explanations (Boix, Acemoglu and Robinson) and that evidence is contested
questions.modelAnswer: Lipset (1959) argued that wealthier societies are more likely to be democratic because development brings education, a middle class and moderation of conflict. This can be read in two ways. The endogenous reading says that development causes transitions to democracy. Przeworski and Limongi (1997) argued that the data support instead the exogenous reading: dictatorships become democracies for many reasons not predicted by income, but once a democracy exists it is much more likely to survive in a rich country. In their data democracies above a certain income level virtually never collapsed. The debate remains live: Boix (2003) and Acemoglu and Robinson (2006) explain democratisation through distributional conflict, in which elites concede democracy to avoid revolution, and critics of Przeworski question the data and the measurement of regimes. A cautious conclusion is that the correlation between wealth and democracy is strong, but the causal story is contested and probably varies across cases.

questions.q: What is Olson's main claim in The Logic of Collective Action (1965)?
options: Large groups with shared interests struggle to organise unless they have selective incentives or coercion
Collective goods can be provided only by state coercion
Larger groups are more effective because there are more contributors
Groups cooperate only when members share an ideology
questions.why: Olson argued that individuals in large groups free-ride, so selective incentives or coercion are needed. The idea that larger groups are more effective is the intuition he challenged. He did not make ideology the key variable. State coercion is only one solution among several, since selective incentives work without it.

questions.q: What did Ostrom's research on common-pool resources show?
options: Cooperation arises only if people are altruistic
Overuse of a commons is inevitable unless it is privatised
Communities can often sustain a shared resource through self-devised rules, monitoring and sanctions
Cooperation is the equilibrium in a one-shot prisoner's dilemma
questions.why: Ostrom's cases show institutions that let communities govern resources without privatisation or central state control. Inevitable overuse is Hardin's pessimistic claim. Her argument concerns institutions and monitoring, not altruism. And in a one-shot prisoner's dilemma the equilibrium is mutual defection, so the claim that cooperation is the one-shot equilibrium is wrong.

questions.q: Why might a rational citizen not vote, and how can turnout be explained?
markScheme: Chance of casting the decisive vote is tiny (Downs 1957)
Calculus of voting pB - C + D > 0 (Riker and Ordeshook 1968)
D term: duty, expressive benefit, social pressure
Other explanations: compulsory voting, mobilisation by parties, social networks
Brief evaluation: rational choice explanations require non-instrumental motives
questions.modelAnswer: Downs (1957) pointed out that in a large electorate the probability that one vote decides the result is almost zero, so if voting has any cost the instrumental benefit seems to be outweighed by the cost. In Riker and Ordeshook's (1968) formulation, a person votes if pB - C + D > 0, where p is the probability of being decisive, B the benefit from the preferred outcome, C the cost of voting and D the satisfaction from duty, expression or belonging. Because pB is tiny, turnout depends mainly on C and D. This explains why changes in costs, such as registration rules, matter and why civic norms are important. Turnout can also be raised by compulsory voting, mobilisation by parties and campaigns, and social pressure from networks. A weakness of the model is that it explains turnout only by adding a term not based on the original instrumental assumption, so some critics think it becomes unfalsifiable.

questions.q: 'Power is an essentially contested concept.' Discuss with reference to the one-, two- and three-dimensional views of power and at least one alternative approach.
markScheme: Introduces the claim and explains contestation (Lukes) of the concept of power
Dahl's first dimension: decision-making, pluralism (Who Governs?)
Bachrach and Baratz: agenda-setting and non-decision-making
Lukes: preference shaping and 'real interests'; criticisms (paternalism, testability)
Alternative: Foucault (productive, diffuse power) or Arendt/Nye/structural power
Evaluates which conception best fits evidence and purposes; considers whether a common core exists
Clear conclusion tied to the question
questions.modelAnswer: Power is often described as an essentially contested concept because there is no neutral definition: rival definitions reflect different views about politics. Dahl (1957) defined power as A's ability to get B to do what B would not otherwise do. In Who Governs? (1961) he operationalised this by studying who prevailed in key decisions in New Haven, finding that different groups won on different issues and concluding that power was pluralistic. This view is clear and empirically tractable but, as Bachrach and Baratz (1962) argued, it misses the power to keep issues off the agenda. Their second dimension, non-decision-making, captures cases where conflicts are suppressed before reaching a decision, a point echoed by Schattschneider's mobilisation of bias. Lukes (1974) argued that even this is incomplete: the most effective exercise of power may be to shape preferences so that conflict never arises. His radical view locates power in ideology, socialisation and the control of information, with the claim that people can be mistaken about their real interests. This is the most ambitious account, but critics see it as paternalistic and hard to test, since we cannot observe what people would want in the absence of power. Alternatives widen the lens. Foucault (1975) saw power as productive and diffuse, operating through norms and disciplinary institutions rather than being held by an agent; this removes the focus on A and B but makes it harder to identify who is responsible. Arendt distinguished power as collective capacity from domination, and Nye's soft power emphasises attraction. These approaches suggest that a single definition may be inadequate. The debate is partly empirical and partly normative: which definition is best depends on what we want the concept to do. Lukes's dimensions can be treated as cumulative, which offers a way of combining them: the first can be studied by observing decisions, the second by studying agendas, and the third by comparing the preferences of people in different circumstances. My conclusion is that power is contested but not arbitrary: the dimensions identify distinct mechanisms, and good analysis specifies which it is studying.

questions.q: To what extent do collective action problems show that states are necessary?
markScheme: Explains collective action problem: free-riding, public goods, prisoner's dilemma
Hobbesian argument: sovereign enforcement as solution
Olson: selective incentives and coercion; role of the state in taxation
Ostrom and Axelrod: cooperation without a state through institutions and repetition
Limits of the state: it faces its own collective action problems; predation (Olson's bandits)
Distinguishes necessary from helpful; scale (global commons, climate)
Reasoned conclusion
questions.modelAnswer: Collective action problems arise when individuals gain from a shared good but each has an incentive to free-ride. In a one-shot prisoner's dilemma defection is dominant, so mutual defection results even though cooperation would benefit all. Hobbes (1651) drew the lesson that only a sovereign able to enforce agreements can secure cooperation. A modern version holds that public goods such as defence and clean air require taxation, since voluntary contributions would be inadequate. Olson (1965) supports this: large groups cannot provide collective goods without selective incentives or coercion, and the state is the principal agent of coercion. However, the claim that states are necessary is too strong. Axelrod (1984) showed cooperation can emerge in repeated interaction through reciprocity, and Ostrom (1990) documented communities that manage common-pool resources through self-devised rules, monitoring and graduated sanctions, often more successfully than central authorities. Such cases depend on features such as small size, clear boundaries and shared norms. The state is also not an automatic solution. Governments face their own collective action problems: officials and interest groups may capture the state, and Olson (1993) noted that rulers may behave as roving bandits as well as stationary ones. International problems such as climate change illustrate the limits, since there is no world state and cooperation relies on agreements that can be evaded; Barrett and others argue enforcement is the central difficulty. This suggests that the state is neither necessary nor sufficient. It is especially helpful for large-scale, anonymous problems where monitoring and sanctions are costly, but communities, markets and norms can substitute where groups are small and interactions repeated. The best answer is that states are one important solution, whose value depends on scale, information and the capacity of the state itself.
